tip: दौड़ता है (daudta hai) = runs, as a routine – not 'is running'. Right-now actions use रहा है (raha hai); the -ता (-ta) form is for habits.
There's no verb 'brush' here – Hindi makes teeth clean: दाँत साफ़ करता हूँ (daant saaf karta hoon). साफ़ (saaf = clean) + करना (karna = do) does the job.
English 'tells' the truth – Hindi speaks it: सच बोलता है (sach bolta hai). Truth and lies both pair with बोलना (bolna = speak), and there's no 'the'.
ये गाड़ियाँ चलती हैं (chalti hain) – literally 'walk'. चलना (chalna) is the verb for machines moving or working: cars, phones and fans all चलते (chalte).
Doubling a word tightens its meaning: सुबह (subah) = morning, सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah) = early in the morning, right at daybreak.
One grandmother, plural verb: दादी जाती हैं (daadi jaati hain), not है (hai). Elders take plural forms as respect – singular would sound rude.
'Studies' is noun + do: पढ़ाई करती है (padhaai karti hai = does studying). Hindi builds many verbs this way – काम करना (kaam karna = to work).
-कर (-kar) chains actions: स्कूल से आकर (school se aakar = having come from school). One small ending replaces the whole phrase 'after coming'.
You arrive 'on' work: काम पर (kaam par) पहुँचता है. पर is literally 'on', but it's the standard word for being at or heading to work.
भी (bhi = also) sits right after the word it highlights: तुम्हारी बहन भी (tumhaari bahan bhi) = your sister too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.
Hindi pairs opposites with a hyphen and skips 'and': दिन-रात (din-raat = day and night). Same pattern in माता-पिता (maata-pita = parents).
वाली (vaali) tags what something comes with: अदरक वाली चाय (adrak vaali chai) = ginger tea, roughly 'the ginger one'. Masculine nouns take वाला (vaala).
'Twice a day' is 'in a day two times': दिन में दो बार (din mein do baar). Everyday Hindi skips 'per' – में (mein = in) plus the time span covers it.
English shops just 'close' – Hindi shops become closed: बंद होती है (band hoti hai = gets closed). A person closing it would be बंद करना (band karna).
'Wear' depends on the item: हेडफ़ोन लगाकर (headphone lagaakar) uses लगाना (lagaana = attach); clothes take पहनना (pahenna). Each item picks its verb.
ठीक (theek) usually means 'fine, okay' – but before a time it means sharp: ठीक छह बजे (theek chhah baje) = at exactly six.
Going somewhere to do something uses the -ने (-ne) verb form: टहलने जाते हैं (tahalne jaate hain) = go for a stroll, literally 'go to stroll'. No 'for' needed.
Hindi has no '-est'. सबसे पहले (sabse pehle) = first of all, literally 'than all, earlier'. सबसे (sabse) + any quality word means 'the most'.
से (se) means 'from' – and also 'by': बस से (bas se) = by bus. Every means of transport takes से; context tells you which sense is meant.
In an 'X और Y' list, दोनों (donon = both) comes at the end: योग और ध्यान दोनों (yog aur dhyaan donon) = both yoga and meditation.
One vowel makes it 'make someone laugh': हँसना (hansna = laugh) → हँसाता (hansaata = makes laugh). No extra 'make' verb – the -आ- (-aa-) does it.
Skills 'come to you': खाना बनाना आता है (khaana banaana aata hai) = literally 'does making food come to you'. Knowing how = the skill + आना (aana = come).
ननिहाल (nanihaal) is one word for 'mother's parents' home' – a classic summer-holiday destination. Hindi has exact words for each side of the family.
रहती (rahti) after another verb means 'keeps on': घूमती रहती है (ghoomti rahti hai) = keeps wandering. रहना (rahna = stay) makes an action ongoing.
सो जाता हूँ (so jaata hoon) = literally 'I go off to sleep'. Adding जाना (jaana = go) marks the change as complete – सोना (sona) alone is just 'sleep'.
'After' comes after: खाने के तुरंत बाद (khaane ke turant baad) = literally 'of eating immediately after'. Time words like बाद (baad) follow their noun.
कम से कम (kam se kam) = at least, literally 'less than less'. Hindi builds it by comparing कम (kam = less) with itself.
देर से आती है (der se aati hai) = comes late, literally 'comes with delay'. देर (der) is a noun – Hindi says 'with delay' where English says 'late'.
